title: Physics: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank
html:
Group A of the NEB Grade 12 Physics paper is eleven one-mark multiple-choice questions. Eleven marks is not much, but they are the quickest marks in the paper and, because the eleven items are spread across the whole syllabus, they punish any unit you skipped. This chapter drills all twenty-five CDC units in syllabus order. Each section opens with a high-yield facts table, then gives eight to ten MCQs, then an answer key in which every answer carries a one-line reason and, where a wrong option encodes a real misconception, names it.

What Group A actually tests

Group A rarely needs a long calculation. It tests four things: a definition or statement, a unit or dimension, one substitution into one formula, or a misconception offered as a distractor. The recent papers have also added graph-reading items (displacement–time graph of SHM, l–T^{2} graph, a cyclic process on a p–V diagram). If an item is eating more than ninety seconds, re-read the question: you have probably missed a word such as maximum, minimum or same.

How the year tags in this chapter work

A tag such as (NEB 2081) is printed only on a question that we saw in that year's board paper; (NEB 2079 model) means the official NEB model question set for 2079, which we downloaded and read. Items tagged like this are reproduced in substance, with the options shortened or reordered. The word data after a tag means that the numbers come from a real past numerical question whose stem has been turned into a one-mark item. The 2078 paper circulates online under two labels (board and model); we tag it (NEB 2078) and note that its label is disputed. Every untagged question is original and built to the same pattern — it is practice, not a leaked paper.

2.1 Rotational dynamics

High-yield fact Value / form
Angular momentum L = I\omega = mvr; unit \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}
Rotational kinetic energy K = \tfrac12 I\omega^{2}; also L = \sqrt{2IK}
Torque \tau = I\alpha = \dfrac{dL}{dt}; work W = \tau\theta; power P = \tau\omega
Radius of gyration I = Mk^{2}, so k = \sqrt{I/M}
Rod, length l, perpendicular axis centre: \dfrac{Ml^{2}}{12}; one end: \dfrac{Ml^{2}}{3}
Equations of angular motion \omega = \omega_0+\alpha t, \theta = \omega_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^{2}, \omega^{2} = \omega_0^{2}+2\alpha\theta
Conservation no external torque \Rightarrow L constant \Rightarrow I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2
  1. The product of the moment of inertia and the angular velocity of a body is its [1] (NEB 2079 model)atorqueblinear momentumcangular momentumdforce
  2. The ratio of the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through one end to that about its centre (both perpendicular to the rod) is [1] (NEB 2082)a2b3c4d6
  3. A flywheel of moment of inertia 2\ \text{kg m}^{2} rotates at 10\ \text{rad s}^{-1}. Its rotational kinetic energy is [1]a20\ \text{J}b40\ \text{J}c100\ \text{J}d200\ \text{J}
  4. A skater spinning with arms outstretched pulls her arms in. Her angular velocity increases because [1]aher angular momentum increasesbher moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum is conservedcher kinetic energy is conservedda torque acts on her
  5. The radius of gyration of a body of mass M and moment of inertia I is [1] (NEB 2078)a\sqrt{MI}b\sqrt{I/M}cI/Md\sqrt{M/I}
  6. A torque of 10\ \text{N m} acts on a wheel of moment of inertia 0.5\ \text{kg m}^{2}. The angular acceleration is [1]a5\ \text{rad s}^{-2}b20\ \text{rad s}^{-2}c0.05\ \text{rad s}^{-2}d2\ \text{rad s}^{-2}
  7. If the rotational kinetic energy of a body is E and its moment of inertia is I, its angular momentum is [1] (NEB 2081)a\sqrt{2IE}b2IEc\sqrt{E/2I}dIE/2
  8. A motor applies a torque of 20\ \text{N m} to a shaft turning at 50\ \text{rad s}^{-1}. The power delivered is [1]a0.4\ \text{W}b70\ \text{W}c2.5\ \text{W}d1000\ \text{W}
  9. A wheel starts from rest with \alpha = 2\ \text{rad s}^{-2}. The angular velocity after turning through 25\ \text{rad} is [1]a5\ \text{rad s}^{-1}b10\ \text{rad s}^{-1}c50\ \text{rad s}^{-1}d100\ \text{rad s}^{-1}
Answers — 2.1

1. (c) — L = I\omega by definition; torque is I\alpha, not I\omega.

2. (c) — \frac{Ml^{2}/3}{Ml^{2}/12} = 4. Students who quote "1/3 versus 1/12" and answer 3 have forgotten to divide.

3. (c) — \tfrac12(2)(10)^{2} = 100\ \text{J}. Option (d) forgets the \tfrac12, option (a) forgets to square \omega.

4. (b) — no external torque, so L = I\omega is fixed; smaller I forces larger \omega. Kinetic energy is not conserved (option c): she does work pulling her arms in, so K rises.

5. (b) — I = Mk^{2}.

6. (b) — \alpha = \tau/I = 10/0.5 = 20. Option (a) multiplies instead of dividing.

7. (a) — E = L^{2}/2I, so L = \sqrt{2IE}.

8. (d) — P = \tau\omega = 20\times50 = 1000\ \text{W}.

9. (b) — \omega^{2} = 2\alpha\theta = 2(2)(25) = 100, so \omega = 10.

2.2 Periodic motion

High-yield fact Value / form
Defining condition of SHM a = -\omega^{2}x (directed to the mean position)
Speed v = \omega\sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}}; maximum v_{max} = \omega A at the mean position
Energy E = \tfrac12 kA^{2} = \tfrac12 m\omega^{2}A^{2}; constant
Spring–mass T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}; independent of g
Simple pendulum T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}; l–T^{2} graph is a straight line of slope 4\pi^{2}/g
Spring cut into n equal parts each part has force constant nk
Resonance driving frequency = natural frequency; amplitude maximum
  1. In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is [1]aconstantbproportional to displacement and directed towards the mean positioncproportional to velocitydzero at the extreme position
  2. A mass of 0.25\ \text{kg} hangs from a spring of force constant 100\ \text{N m}^{-1}. Its time period is [1]a0.31\ \text{s}b0.63\ \text{s}c3.14\ \text{s}d6.28\ \text{s}
  3. At the mean position of a particle in SHM [1]akinetic energy is minimumbpotential energy is maximumcspeed is maximum and acceleration is zerodspeed and acceleration are both maximum
  4. A simple pendulum is taken to the Moon, where g is one-sixth of its value on Earth. Its time period [1]abecomes 6 timesbbecomes \sqrt{6} timescbecomes 1/\sqrt{6} timesdis unchanged
  5. A particle of mass 0.5\ \text{kg} is attached to a spring of force constant 200\ \text{N m}^{-1} and oscillates with amplitude 0.1\ \text{m}. The total energy is [1]a0.5\ \text{J}b1\ \text{J}c2\ \text{J}d10\ \text{J}
  6. A uniform spring is cut into two equal halves. The force constant and the frequency of each half (for the same mass) are [1] (NEB 2080)ahalved; halvedbdoubled; multiplied by \sqrt{2}cdoubled; doubleddunchanged; unchanged
  7. A simple pendulum bob of mass 0.40\ \text{kg} has potential energy 0.044\ \text{J} at an extreme point, taking the mean point as reference. Its kinetic energy at the mean point is [1] (NEB 2079 model)a0.022\ \text{J}b0.044\ \text{J}c0.011\ \text{J}d0.033\ \text{J}
  8. The time period of a simple pendulum inside an orbiting satellite is [1]azerobthe same as on Earthcinfinite, because effective g is zeroddoubled
  9. A particle of amplitude 0.02\ \text{m} oscillates in SHM with frequency 5\ \text{Hz}. Its maximum speed is [1]a0.10\ \text{m s}^{-1}b0.63\ \text{m s}^{-1}c6.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}d0.20\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  10. Resonance occurs when [1]athe driving force is very largebdamping is zerocthe driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the systemdthe amplitude of the driver is maximum
Answers — 2.2

1. (b) — a = -\omega^{2}x. At the extreme position acceleration is maximum, which is why (d) is wrong.

2. (a) — T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.25/100} = 2\pi(0.05) = 0.314\ \text{s}. Option (c) forgets the square root.

3. (c) — at x = 0: v = \omega A (maximum), a = 0, K maximum, U minimum.

4. (b) — T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}, so T increases by \sqrt{6}. Option (a) treats T as proportional to 1/g.

5. (b) — E = \tfrac12kA^{2} = \tfrac12(200)(0.1)^{2} = 1\ \text{J}. The mass does not enter.

6. (b) — a half-length spring is stiffer: k' = 2k, so f' = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{2k/m} = \sqrt{2}f.

7. (b) — energy is conserved at every point of the swing, so K_{mean} = U_{extreme} = 0.044\ \text{J}; the mass, time period and amplitude are red herrings.

8. (c) — in free fall the effective g is zero, so T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\to\infty: the pendulum does not oscillate. (A spring–mass system would be unaffected, because T does not contain g.)

9. (b) — v_{max} = \omega A = 2\pi(5)(0.02) = 0.63\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Option (d) uses \omega = f.

10. (c) — resonance is a frequency match; amplitude of the driver or absence of damping is not the condition (zero damping would only make the peak infinite).

2.3 Fluid statics

High-yield fact Value / form
Pressure at depth P = P_0+\rho gh; gauge pressure \rho gh
Surface energy E = T\,\Delta A; soap bubble has two surfaces
Capillary rise h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}; h\propto 1/r, h\propto 1/g
Stokes' law; terminal velocity F = 6\pi\eta rv; v_t = \dfrac{2r^{2}(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}\propto r^{2}
Poiseuille \dfrac{V}{t} = \dfrac{\pi Pr^{4}}{8\eta l}
Continuity; Bernoulli A_1v_1 = A_2v_2; P+\tfrac12\rho v^{2}+\rho gh = constant
Floating body \dfrac{\text{submerged volume}}{\text{total volume}} = \dfrac{\rho_{body}}{\rho_{liquid}}
  1. Two capillary tubes of radii 4\ \text{mm} and 2\ \text{mm} are dipped in the same liquid. The ratio of the heights of rise in them is [1] (NEB 2081)a1:2b2:1c1:4d4:1
  2. If the height of capillary rise in a tube on the Earth is h, the height on the Moon (g_{Moon} = g/6) is [1] (NEB 2078)ah/6bhc6hd36h
  3. Two identical raindrops, each falling at a terminal velocity of 0.15\ \text{m s}^{-1}, combine into one drop. The new terminal velocity is about [1] (NEB 2082)a0.15\ \text{m s}^{-1}b0.24\ \text{m s}^{-1}c0.30\ \text{m s}^{-1}d0.60\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  4. The work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius 2\ \text{cm} (surface tension 0.03\ \text{N m}^{-1}) is about [1]a1.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}b3.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}c6.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}d3.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{J}
  5. Water flows at 2\ \text{m s}^{-1} through a pipe of cross-section 200\ \text{cm}^{2} into a section of 50\ \text{cm}^{2}. The speed in the narrow section is [1]a0.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}b2\ \text{m s}^{-1}c4\ \text{m s}^{-1}d8\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  6. A stream of air is blown horizontally underneath one pan of a beam balance. That pan [1] (NEB 2078)agoes downbgoes upcstays leveldoscillates about the level
  7. If the radius of a horizontal capillary tube is doubled, the rate of flow of a liquid under the same pressure difference becomes [1]a2 timesb4 timesc8 timesd16 times
  8. A block floats in water with three-quarters of its volume submerged. Its relative density is [1]a0.25b0.50c0.75d1.33
  9. The gauge pressure at a depth of 10\ \text{m} in water (\rho = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}, g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}) is [1]a9.8\times10^{3}\ \text{Pa}b9.8\times10^{4}\ \text{Pa}c1.98\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}d1.01\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}
Answers — 2.3

1. (a) — h\propto 1/r, so the wider tube gives the smaller rise: \dfrac{h_{4}}{h_{2}} = \dfrac{r_{2}}{r_{4}} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 1:2. Option (b) inverts the ratio.

2. (c) — h\propto 1/g; weaker gravity means the column climbs six times higher.

3. (b) — volume doubles so r' = 2^{1/3}r; v_t\propto r^{2} gives v' = 2^{2/3}(0.15) = 0.24\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Option (c) wrongly assumes v_t\propto volume.

4. (b) — a bubble has two surfaces: W = T\times2\times4\pi r^{2} = 0.03\times2\times4\pi(0.02)^{2} = 3.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}. Option (a) counts one surface only.

5. (d) — A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 gives v_2 = 200\times2/50 = 8\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Option (a) divides the wrong way.

6. (a) — the air moving under the pan has lower pressure (Bernoulli), so the still air above pushes the pan down. Students who answer (b) picture the moving air "lifting" the pan.

7. (d) — V/t\propto r^{4}, so 2^{4} = 16.

8. (c) — fraction submerged =\rho_{body}/\rho_{water} = 0.75.

9. (b) — \rho gh = 1000\times9.8\times10 = 9.8\times10^{4}\ \text{Pa}; option (d) is the atmospheric pressure, which is not part of the gauge value.

2.4 First Law of Thermodynamics

High-yield fact Value / form
First law Q = \Delta U + W; \Delta U of an ideal gas depends on temperature only
Work W = \int P\,dV = area under the p–V curve; isobaric W = P\Delta V
Isothermal PV = constant; W = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}; \Delta U = 0
Adiabatic Q = 0; PV^{\gamma} = constant; W = \dfrac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}
Isochoric W = 0; Q = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T; P\propto T
Heat capacities C_P - C_V = R; \gamma = C_P/C_V (\tfrac53 monatomic, \tfrac75 diatomic)
Work for the same expansion, same initial state isobaric > isothermal > adiabatic > isochoric (=0)
  1. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on [1] (NEB 2079 model)avolume onlybpressure onlyctemperature onlydboth pressure and volume
  2. A gas expands from the same initial state through the same volume change by four different processes. The work done by the gas is greatest in the [1] (NEB 2079 model)aisothermal processbisobaric processcadiabatic processdisochoric process
  3. A gas in a rigid vessel is heated from 127\ ^{\circ}\text{C} to 227\ ^{\circ}\text{C}. The ratio of initial to final pressure is [1] (NEB 2081)a127:227b4:5c5:4d1:1
  4. In an adiabatic process [1] (NEB 2082)atemperature stays constantbno heat enters or leaves the systemcpressure stays constantdvolume stays constant
  5. A gas at constant pressure 2\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa} expands from 1\ \text{L} to 3\ \text{L}. The work done by the gas is [1]a200\ \text{J}b400\ \text{J}c600\ \text{J}d4\times10^{5}\ \text{J}
  6. A system absorbs 500\ \text{J} of heat and does 200\ \text{J} of work. Its internal energy [1]arises by 700\ \text{J}brises by 300\ \text{J}cfalls by 300\ \text{J}dis unchanged
  7. One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally at 300\ \text{K} to double its volume. The heat absorbed is about (R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}) [1]a1.2\ \text{kJ}b1.7\ \text{kJ}c2.5\ \text{kJ}d3.4\ \text{kJ}
  8. A monatomic ideal gas (\gamma = \tfrac53) is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. The pressure becomes [1]a8 timesb16 timesc32 timesd64 times
  9. Which relation between the molar heat capacities of an ideal gas is correct? [1]aC_V - C_P = RbC_P + C_V = RcC_P - C_V = RdC_P/C_V = R
Answers — 2.4

1. (c) — for an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so U is purely the kinetic energy, which depends on T alone. Option (d) is the classic confusion with a real gas.

2. (b) — between the same two volumes the isobaric path lies highest on the p–V diagram, the isochoric path has zero area. (The item is about expansion from the same state; with different end-points the ranking can change.)

3. (b) — P\propto T at constant volume with T in kelvin: 400:500 = 4:5. Option (a) uses Celsius temperatures.

4. (b) — Q = 0. Temperature changes in an adiabatic process (it is the isothermal one that holds T constant).

5. (b) — W = P\Delta V = 2\times10^{5}\times2\times10^{-3} = 400\ \text{J}. Option (d) forgets to convert litres to cubic metres.

6. (b) — \Delta U = Q - W = 500 - 200 = +300\ \text{J}. Option (a) adds instead of subtracting.

7. (b) — isothermal, so Q = W = RT\ln2 = 8.31\times300\times0.693 = 1.73\ \text{kJ}.

8. (c) — P_2/P_1 = (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma} = 8^{5/3} = 32. Option (a) treats it as isothermal (\gamma = 1).

9. (c) — Mayer's relation. C_P exceeds C_V because at constant pressure the gas also does expansion work.

2.5 Second Law of Thermodynamics

High-yield fact Value / form
Kelvin–Planck no engine can convert all the heat it takes from a single reservoir into work
Clausius heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body
Efficiency \eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = 1-\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}; Carnot \eta = 1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} (kelvin)
Refrigerator \text{COP} = \dfrac{Q_2}{W} = \dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2} = \dfrac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}
Otto cycle \eta = 1-\dfrac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}, r = compression ratio
Diesel vs petrol diesel has the higher compression ratio (about 15–22 against 6–10)
Entropy \Delta S = \dfrac{Q}{T} for a reversible step; an isolated system never loses entropy
  1. The efficiency of a Carnot engine working between the steam point and the ice point is about [1] (NEB 2082)a10\%b27\%c73\%d100\%
  2. A heat engine takes 500\ \text{J} from the source and rejects 400\ \text{J} to the sink. Its efficiency is [1]a80\%b25\%c20\%d10\%
  3. The coefficient of performance of an ideal refrigerator working between 273\ \text{K} and 300\ \text{K} is about [1] (NEB 2078)a0.1b1.1c10d27
  4. The efficiency of an Otto engine with compression ratio 8 and \gamma = 1.4 is about [1]a43\%b57\%c75\%d88\%
  5. A Carnot engine has a sink at 300\ \text{K} and an efficiency of 50\%. The source temperature is [1]a450\ \text{K}b600\ \text{K}c900\ \text{K}d150\ \text{K}
  6. The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law says that [1](a) heat flows from hot to cold(b) no cyclic engine can be 100\% efficient when working from a single reservoir(c) energy is conserved(d) entropy of the universe is constant
  7. Which of the following has the higher compression ratio? [1]apetrol enginebdiesel enginecboth the samedsteam engine
  8. The entropy of an isolated system undergoing an irreversible process [1]adecreasesbremains constantcincreasesdbecomes zero
  9. A refrigerator absorbs 200\ \text{J} from the cold space using 50\ \text{J} of work. The heat rejected to the room is [1]a150\ \text{J}b250\ \text{J}c200\ \text{J}d4\ \text{J}
Answers — 2.5

1. (b) — \eta = 1 - 273/373 = 0.268. Option (c) is T_2/T_1, the rejected fraction.

2. (c) — \eta = 1 - 400/500 = 20\%; option (a) is Q_2/Q_1.

3. (c) — \text{COP} = 273/(300-273) = 10.1. The refrigerator works between a cold space at the ice point and the room; a value above 1 is normal for a refrigerator, unlike an engine.

4. (b) — \eta = 1 - 8^{-0.4} = 1 - 0.435 = 0.565.

5. (b) — 0.5 = 1 - 300/T_1 gives T_1 = 600\ \text{K}.

6. (b) — this is the statement itself; (a) is Clausius's statement in weakened form, (c) is the first law.

7. (b) — a diesel engine compresses air alone, so it can run at a high ratio without pre-ignition; a petrol engine compresses fuel vapour and would knock.

8. (c) — the direction of spontaneous change is the direction in which entropy of the isolated system rises.

9. (b) — energy balance: Q_1 = Q_2 + W = 200 + 50 = 250\ \text{J}. Option (a) subtracts.

2.6 Wave motion

High-yield fact Value / form
Wave speed v = f\lambda = \omega/k
Travelling wave along +x y = A\sin(\omega t - kx), k = 2\pi/\lambda
Phase difference \Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x
Two consecutive particles in the same phase \lambda apart
Stationary wave nodes and antinodes each \lambda/2 apart; node–antinode \lambda/4
Superposition resultant displacement = algebraic sum of displacements
  1. The distance between two consecutive particles of a wave that are in the same phase is [1] (NEB 2081)a\lambda/4b\lambda/2c\lambdad2\lambda
  2. A wave is described by y = 0.05\sin(40t - 2x) in SI units. Its speed is [1]a2\ \text{m s}^{-1}b20\ \text{m s}^{-1}c40\ \text{m s}^{-1}d80\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  3. Two points on a wave of wavelength 2\ \text{m} are 0.5\ \text{m} apart. Their phase difference is [1]a\pi/4b\pi/2c\pid2\pi
  4. Which of the following is a transverse wave? [1] (NEB 2082)asound in airba pulse on a stretched stringca compression in a springdsound in water
  5. Two pulses of +2\ \text{cm} and +3\ \text{cm} meet exactly over each other on a string. The displacement at that instant is [1]a1\ \text{cm}b2.5\ \text{cm}c5\ \text{cm}d6\ \text{cm}
  6. A stationary wave of frequency 100\ \text{Hz} is set up in air where the speed of sound is 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Adjacent nodes are separated by [1]a0.85\ \text{m}b1.7\ \text{m}c3.4\ \text{m}d6.8\ \text{m}
  7. In a stationary wave all particles between two consecutive nodes [1]ahave the same amplitudebvibrate in the same phase with different amplitudescare at restdvibrate in opposite phase
  8. A source of frequency 500\ \text{Hz} produces waves of wavelength 0.68\ \text{m}. The wave speed is [1]a170\ \text{m s}^{-1}b340\ \text{m s}^{-1}c735\ \text{m s}^{-1}d0.00136\ \text{m s}^{-1}
Answers — 2.6

1. (c) — same phase means a phase difference of 2\pi, i.e. one wavelength. Option (b) is the node-to-node spacing in a stationary wave.

2. (b) — v = \omega/k = 40/2 = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Option (c) quotes \omega directly.

3. (b) — \Delta\phi = 2\pi(0.5)/2 = \pi/2.

4. (b) — the string's particles move perpendicular to the direction of travel. Sound in fluids is always longitudinal.

5. (c) — superposition: add the displacements algebraically, 2+3 = 5\ \text{cm}.

6. (b) — \lambda = v/f = 3.4\ \text{m}; nodes are \lambda/2 = 1.7\ \text{m} apart. Option (c) gives the wavelength itself.

7. (b) — that is the defining feature of a stationary wave: a common phase within each loop, with the amplitude varying from zero at the nodes to maximum at the antinode.

8. (b) — v = f\lambda = 500\times0.68 = 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

2.7 Mechanical waves

High-yield fact Value / form
Solid v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}
Liquid v = \sqrt{K/\rho}
Gas, Newton (isothermal) v = \sqrt{P/\rho}, about 280\ \text{m s}^{-1} at 0 °C — too low
Gas, Laplace (adiabatic) v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}, about 332\ \text{m s}^{-1} at 0 °C
Temperature v\propto\sqrt{T}; v_t \approx v_0 + 0.61\,t (t in °C)
Pressure no effect at constant temperature (P/\rho constant)
Humidity moist air is less dense, so sound is faster
  1. A change in atmospheric pressure, at constant temperature, affects the velocity of sound in air [1]aby doubling itbnot at allcin proportion to \sqrt{P}din proportion to P
  2. Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air gives a value of about [1]a280\ \text{m s}^{-1}b332\ \text{m s}^{-1}c380\ \text{m s}^{-1}d3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  3. Laplace's correction replaced the isothermal assumption by [1] (NEB 2080, 2081)athe isobaric assumptionbthe adiabatic assumptioncthe isochoric assumptionda constant-density assumption
  4. Taking 332\ \text{m s}^{-1} at 0\ ^{\circ}\text{C} and 0.61\ \text{m s}^{-1} per degree, the speed of sound at 27\ ^{\circ}\text{C} is about [1]a316\ \text{m s}^{-1}b332\ \text{m s}^{-1}c348\ \text{m s}^{-1}d359\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  5. The speed of a longitudinal wave in steel (Y = 2\times10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}, \rho = 8000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}) is [1]a500\ \text{m s}^{-1}b1580\ \text{m s}^{-1}c5000\ \text{m s}^{-1}d25000\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  6. Which property of sound changes when the temperature of the air changes (source frequency fixed)? [1] (NEB 2079 model)aamplitudebfrequencycwavelengthdintensity
  7. If the absolute temperature of a gas is raised from 300\ \text{K} to 1200\ \text{K}, the speed of sound in it [1]adoublesbquadrupleschalvesdis unchanged
  8. Sound travels faster in moist air than in dry air because [1]awater vapour raises the pressurebmoist air is less densecmoist air is colderdhumidity raises the frequency

Chapter summary

  • Group A of the NEB Grade 12 Physics paper is eleven one-mark items drawn from across all twenty-five units; no unit is safe to skip, which is why this chapter gives every unit its own facts table, its own MCQs and its own reasoned key.
  • Recent papers repeat a small core of Group A facts: the angular momentum product I\omega; energy conservation in SHM; capillary rise and raindrop terminal velocity (v_t\propto r^{2}); the work ranking of thermodynamic processes; Carnot efficiency in kelvin; node–antinode spacing; Laplace's adiabatic correction; thermocouple \theta_i = 2\theta_n-\theta_c; Lenz's law and energy; the peak of the 220\ \text{V} supply (311\ \text{V}); the focus of an earthquake.
  • Most lost marks are unit slips, not physics slips: \text{cm}^{2} left unconverted, Celsius used in gas laws, kelvin under a square root, \text{eV} and joule mixed, the \tfrac12 omitted in \tfrac12LI^{2} and \tfrac12I\omega^{2}.
  • Formula pairs that are confused: closed-pipe v/4L against open-pipe v/2L; observer-moving against source-moving Doppler; Malus' \cos^{2}\theta against \cos\theta; B at the centre of a coil (\mu_0NI/2r) against a straight wire (\mu_0I/2\pi d); I^{2}Rt against IRt.
  • Graph items are now common: read the slope of l–T^{2} (4\pi^{2}/g), of K_{max}–f (h), the area of a p–V loop (work) and of a hysteresis loop (energy loss per cycle).
